terms.definition: A working molecule built by cells out of a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific 3D shape to do a job.
terms.function: Does the physical work of the cell and body — cutting, carrying, signaling, or building — based on the specific shape it folds into.
terms.whereItIs: Built inside cells by ribosomes, then used throughout the body wherever that particular job needs doing.
terms.whyItMatters: Proteins are why the body actually works, not just what it's made of — digestion, healing, immunity, and movement all depend on proteins doing their jobs correctly.

terms.definition: A protein starts as a long chain of amino acids strung together like beads, in an order set by a gene.
terms.function: Serves as the raw, unfolded sequence of building blocks that folding will shape into the protein's working 3D form.
terms.whereItIs: The loose, unfolded tail near the model's N-terminus, before the chain folds into the compact core.
terms.whyItMatters: There are 20 different kinds of amino acid 'beads,' and the exact sequence determines everything that happens next, including the final shape and function.

terms.definition: The chain twists and folds into coils (alpha helices) and pleats (beta sheets), then packs into one specific compact 3D shape.
terms.function: Converts the 1D amino acid chain into a precise, stable 3D structure that can physically interact with other molecules.
terms.whereItIs: The dense folded core at the model's center, where helices and sheets pack together into the compact globule.
terms.whyItMatters: Folding happens automatically based on how amino acids attract and repel each other; getting the fold right is the difference between a working protein and one that can't do its job.

terms.definition: The folded shape creates pockets and surfaces that fit specific molecules, like a lock fits a key.
terms.function: Gives the protein its specific job — an enzyme's pocket fits its target molecule, an antibody's arms fit a specific germ.
terms.whereItIs: A distinct pocket, groove, or cleft on the folded core's surface, where the shape creates a specific-fitting slot.
terms.whyItMatters: This shape is exactly why a protein can do its job — without the right shape, correct amino acids alone aren't enough.

terms.definition: Every protein is built by following instructions copied from a gene in DNA.
terms.function: Specifies the exact order of amino acids used to build this protein's chain, which then determines its fold and function.
terms.whereItIs: A dot on the chain's starting end (N-terminus), the same point where the amino acid chain begins.
terms.whyItMatters: A single change in the gene's instructions can change the amino acid sequence — and therefore the shape and function — of the protein it builds.

terms.definition: A small molecule that acts like one bead on a chain; amino acids link together in long chains to build proteins.
terms.function: Acts as the single building-block unit that, strung together in sequence, forms a protein's amino acid chain.
terms.whereItIs: Linked end-to-end along the entire length of a protein's backbone, before and after folding.
terms.whyItMatters: There are 20 different amino acids, and which ones are used, and in what order, is what makes every protein different from every other protein.

terms.definition: The process by which a freshly made chain of amino acids bends and twists itself into a specific compact 3D shape.
terms.function: Turns a simple, linear chain of amino acids into the precise 3D structure the protein needs to do its job.
terms.whereItIs: Happens as soon as the amino acid chain is built by a ribosome, often folding as it's still being assembled.
terms.whyItMatters: A protein cannot function until it folds correctly; misfolded proteins are linked to diseases in the body.

terms.definition: A section of DNA that contains the instructions for building one specific protein.
terms.function: Spells out, through its DNA sequence, the exact order of amino acids a cell should string together to build one protein.
terms.whereItIs: A specific stretch of DNA, packed inside chromosomes, inside the nucleus of a cell.
terms.whyItMatters: Genes are the original source of every protein's instructions — no gene, no protein.

terms.definition: The cell structure that reads genetic instructions and links amino acids together to build a protein.
terms.function: Reads a copied gene instruction (messenger RNA) and physically links amino acids together in the order that instruction specifies.
terms.whereItIs: Found floating in a cell's cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.
terms.whyItMatters: The ribosome is the actual construction site where a protein's amino acid chain gets built, turning genetic instructions into a real physical molecule.

terms.definition: A type of protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the body, like a helper that makes reactions happen faster.
terms.function: Uses its folded shape's binding pocket to grab a target molecule and speed up a specific chemical reaction involving it.
terms.whereItIs: Found throughout the body wherever a chemical reaction needs a speed boost, such as in digestion.
terms.whyItMatters: Enzymes are a clear, concrete example of shape-determines-function: an enzyme's pocket only fits its intended target molecule.

terms.definition: A change in a gene's DNA sequence that can change the amino acid chain, and sometimes the shape and function, of the protein it builds.
terms.function: Alters the instructions a gene provides, which can change which amino acid gets placed at a given position in the chain.
terms.whereItIs: Occurs within the DNA sequence of a gene, before that gene's instructions are ever copied and used.
terms.whyItMatters: A single mutation can be harmless, or it can break a protein's fold and function entirely, which is why mutations matter so much in genetics and disease.
